versions.text:
I had promised Ms. Reyes four dozen oatmeal cookies for our class bake sale on Saturday, so bringing them was my job. Grandma Bea left her recipe card on the counter and asked if I wanted help, but I told her I could do the work myself.

The card said to use softened butter, but the butter had set hard in the refrigerator, and waiting for it would take an hour. To save time, I melted it in the microwave, which seemed like a clever shortcut. The first tray came out as one flat, greasy sheet. It was a mistake, and it was far from perfect.

Grandma watched from the doorway without a word. A few minutes later Ana came over with the sign she had painted for our table. 'You can still save it,' she said. 'Break it into pieces and call them oat crisps. They might sell even better.' I shook my head at the ruined tray. 'That skips fixing what went wrong,' I said. 'It just gives the mistake a new name.'

The rest of the dough was as runny as soup, so I scraped it into the trash and started a new batch, waiting this time for the butter to soften. Grandma came in once, tapped the words softened butter on the card, and went to bed. I had tried to save an hour, and it was past eleven when the last tray came out.

On Saturday the buyers emptied our table by ten. Ms. Reyes took a bite, raised her eyebrows, and said, 'Whoever baked these took their time.' I laughed, because she had no idea how much, and that night I printed two words across the top of the recipe card: SOFTENED BUTTER.

I had promised Ms. Reyes four dozen oatmeal cookies for our class bake sale on Saturday, so bringing them was my job. Grandma Bea left her recipe card on the counter and asked if I wanted help, and I told her I would ask if the work got difficult.

The card said to use softened butter, but the butter was still hard from the refrigerator. To save time, I melted it in the microwave, which seemed like a clever shortcut. I set the first tray on the stove and stared at one flat sheet, thin as paper and brown at the edges. It was a mistake, and it was far from perfect.

Grandma watched from the doorway, and soon she had snapped off a corner of the sheet and was reaching for another piece. A few minutes later Ana came over with the sign she had painted for our table. 'You can still save it,' she said. 'Break it into pieces and call them oat crisps. They might sell even better.' I looked at the ruined tray, crunchy and easy to package. 'That could save the whole batch,' I said.

I had planned to fix what went wrong and start again. Instead, we baked the rest of the dough the same flat way, on purpose this time, and broke every sheet into pieces. We were finished by eight, earlier than round cookies would have taken.

On Saturday the oat crisps were the first thing gone from our table, and buyers came back for more. Ms. Reyes held up an empty bag and asked, 'Could you make these again for the spring festival?' That night I wrote a new title on the back of the recipe card: OAT CRISPS.

I had promised Ms. Reyes four dozen oatmeal cookies for our class bake sale on Saturday, so bringing them was my job. Grandma Bea left her recipe card on the counter and asked if I wanted help. 'It's my job,' I said. 'I can do the work myself.'

The card said to use softened butter, but the butter was still hard from the refrigerator. To save time, I melted it in the microwave, which seemed like a clever shortcut. I slid in the first tray and set the timer for twelve minutes, and when it beeped, the cookies had melted into one flat, greasy sheet. It was a mistake, and it was far from perfect.

Grandma watched from the doorway with her apron already tied. A few minutes later Ana came over with the sign she had painted for our table. 'You can still save it,' she said. 'Break it into pieces and call them oat crisps. They might sell even better.' When she reached for a knife, I pulled the ruined tray toward me and thought, First Grandma, now Ana. 'I've got it,' I said.

I tried to fix what went wrong by myself, but extra flour only made the next tray lumpy and just as flat. By nine, saying 'Can you help me?' took three tries. Grandma had the bowl in the freezer before I finished the sentence, and twenty minutes later the next batch came out round. After that, the work went quickly.

On Saturday the buyers emptied our table by ten. Ms. Reyes asked, 'Did you bake all four dozen by yourself?' 'No,' I said. 'Grandma and I did.' That night I wrote two words at the bottom of the recipe card: ASK EARLY.

I had promised Ms. Reyes four dozen oatmeal cookies for our class bake sale on Saturday, so bringing them was my job. Grandma Bea left her recipe card on the counter and asked if I wanted help, but I told her I could do the work myself.

I had set myself a goal of forty-eight cookies, every one of them perfect. The card said to use softened butter, but the butter was still hard from the refrigerator, so to save time I melted it in the microwave, which seemed like a clever shortcut. The first tray came out flat, the cookies spread wide and touching. It was a mistake, and an embarrassing one.

Grandma watched from the doorway. A few minutes later Ana came over with the sign she had painted for our table. 'You can still save it,' she said. 'Break it into pieces and call them oat crisps. They might sell even better.' I frowned at the ruined tray. 'I promised cookies,' I said. 'Not crumbs in a bag.'

I tried to fix what went wrong by baking the rest of the batch in small, careful spoonfuls, but only twenty came out round. I boxed those and pushed the flat ones toward the trash. When I looked up, Grandma had stuck a strip of tape on the big tin by the front door that said Ms. Reyes, 4 dozen. I stood there a long time, then I packed every cookie, flat ones too.

On Saturday two families had dropped out of the sale, and our table looked half empty until I opened the tin. Ms. Reyes counted. 'Forty-eight. That is exactly what we needed.' The buyers took the flat ones as quickly as the round ones.
